shared_text:
The flight. A narrow-body airliner arriving at an airport with thunderstorms nearby. Daytime, instrument conditions.

The crew. The captain was the pilot flying and the first officer the pilot monitoring. On the last day of a four-day trip, after minimum rest, both were fit for duty but reported fatigue.

What happened. The crew had briefed the forecast storms. Levelling at 3,000 ft, with flaps 5 and speed brakes out for ATC's step-down restrictions, the crew learned the wind had reversed and was gusty. Concerned about tailwind limits, the captain accepted the opposite-direction approach; ATC gave a turn and climb to 6,000 ft. The first officer set a 700 ft per minute climb in vertical speed mode, but both pilots saw at once it was not climbing. The captain disconnected the autopilot, added thrust and pitched up, and the flaps went to 1. With barely a positive climb, the first officer saw the speed brakes still extended, and they were retracted. ATC then assigned 4,000 ft. On final approach, with the airport hidden by cloud, no current field conditions and a storm cell over it on radar, the captain went around. In cloud, heavy rain, moderate turbulence and lightning, the captain turned right at once, away from the weather; ATC approved. A gust rolled the aircraft to about 35 degrees of bank; the captain corrected it. As the flaps came up from 10 to 5 and 1, the speed rose quickly, exceeding the flap limit by about 15 knots.
safe_outcome: The airspeed was stabilised, and the aircraft levelled at 3,000 ft on a heading from ATC. After leaving the weather the crew held south of the airport; after two turns the weather cleared, and they landed after a second approach. Maintenance inspected the flaps for the overspeed and found no abnormalities. There was no conflict with other traffic. No one was hurt and the aircraft was not damaged.
bad_outcome: Another aircraft was crossing nearby. Both crews received TCAS resolution advisories and followed them, and the aircraft passed about 300 feet vertically and half a mile apart. A flight attendant on this aircraft was thrown against a galley cart during the manoeuvre and received a minor injury.
notes: Removed under rule 3: the whole debrief paragraph (task saturation, tunnel vision, 'delayed mental processing', the view that level change mode would have been better than vertical speed, that the speed brakes should have been checked, that the go-around should have been more deliberate, that a hold should have been requested, and the credit to teamwork and CRM). The fatigue facts (last day of a four-day trip, minimum rest, fit for duty, reported fatigue) are kept as the crew's state at the time. Moved under rule 5: stabilising the airspeed, levelling at 3,000 ft, the hold, the second approach and landing, and the flap inspection result. Removed under rule 6: airport names, runway numbers and fix names. Cut for length (at-the-time facts; the report is long): the previous day's maintenance delay, the en-route turbulence and altitude changes, holding advised then lifted, the vectors between cells to the east and west, an earlier runway change because of debris, the FMC reprogramming after each runway change, the increasing speed as the reason for flaps 1, re-engaging the autopilot and VNAV at 4,000 ft (a couple of attempts while trimming), losing sight of the airport and the captain briefly mistaking a nearby airport for it, the last arrival reporting light rain and the crew being the first to land from the south, the first officer telling ATC an immediate turn was needed, gear up in the go-around, and the brief bank angle alert. Judgement calls: the report has two deviation episodes (not climbing to the assigned 6,000 ft with speed brakes extended, and the flap overspeed in the go-around); both are kept and the text stops at the overspeed. Bracket 'crossing': the aircraft made an unplanned right turn off the go-around path in weather, where other aircraft could be crossing.
